title: Escalation Rules: Escalation Chain, Agent-Level Triggers, and Human Gate Conditions
body:
These rules govern when and how agents escalate. No agent may deviate based on convenience, time pressure, or a judgment that a different path would be faster. This file takes precedence over per-agent escalation trigger descriptions.

**Five Escalation Principles:**

**Principle 1: Escalation goes up the chain, not sideways.** Agents escalate to the agent above them in the hierarchy, not to peer agents. section-drafter escalates to lead-orchestrator, not to lead-editor. Sideways escalation bypasses the orchestration layer and creates untracked state changes. It is forbidden. The only exception is routing a blocker_report to blockage-handler — but this is not a peer escalation; blockage-handler feeds back to lead-orchestrator.

**Principle 2: Every escalation produces a structured artifact.** No silent failures. No verbal escalations. No escalation by omission (stopping work without documentation). Every escalation produces either: a blocker_report.json (for blockers requiring classification and a resume plan), or a flagged output with a populated issues field. Both must comply with their schemas.

**Principle 3: Escalation does not stop unblocked work.** When an agent encounters a blocker and escalates, it continues all work not downstream of the blocker. An agent that halts all work because one section is blocked has failed its escalation obligation.

**Principle 4: Escalation thresholds are defined per agent.** 'Use judgment' is not a valid escalation threshold. If an agent encounters a situation not covered by its defined triggers, classify using the B1-B9 taxonomy, determine the closest matching trigger, and note in the blocker_report that the trigger required classification judgment.

**Principle 5: Escalation level determines routing.** An agent that bypasses Level 2 to route directly to Level 4 (the human gate) when a Level 2 resolution would suffice has violated the escalation protocol.

**Four Escalation Levels:**

**Level 1 — Within-agent self-resolution:** Applies when a reasonable default exists, the decision is inferable from context, the error is correctable within the agent's own scope, and the issue does not affect other agents' inputs. The agent applies the inference, logs it as a Type 2 assumption, continues work. Does not ask the user, does not stop work, does not route to blockage-handler.

**Level 2 — Agent → blockage-handler:** Applies when a B-type blocker has been identified, is scoped to some but not all work, blocked work can resume when the blocker is resolved, and resolution does not require a user decision. Agent classifies the blocker, produces all unblocked outputs, produces a blocker_report.json with complete resume plan, routes to blockage-handler, continues all unblocked work.

**Level 3 — blockage-handler → lead-orchestrator:** Applies when the resolution requires either a human gate trigger or an alternate workflow path that only lead-orchestrator can authorize. Examples: B1 (missing user decision) not inferable; B8 (contradictory instructions) not resolvable by priority; multiple overlapping blockers cover more than 50% of planned output.

**Level 4 — lead-orchestrator → Human Gate:** Applies when Gate 1 (required input missing), Gate 2 (consequential ambiguity), Gate 3 (doctrine conflict), Gate 4 (canon conflict), or Gate 5 (destructive operation) conditions are met. lead-orchestrator produces the gate-format output, states the default action clearly, continues all unblocked branches while waiting, logs the gate trigger.

**Human Gate Trigger Conditions:**
- HG-1 (Gate 1): two or more competent agents would reach opposite conclusions; the conclusions produce documents that serve different readers or purposes; no context supports one conclusion over the other.
- HG-2 (Gate 3 Doctrine Conflict): user instruction explicitly contradicts a non-negotiable doctrine rule (not just a preference or default).
- HG-3 (Quality Gate BLOCK): blocking issue cannot be resolved by any combination of revision passes — requires scope change, brief amendment, or canon update.
- HG-4 (Brief Scope Change): draft requires significantly more content than the brief defines, or discovery reveals a prerequisite topic the brief omits.
- HG-5 (Gate 5 Destructive Operation): any operation that irreversibly overwrites, deletes, or replaces existing completed work — no exceptions.

**Escalation Anti-Patterns:** (1) Escalating an inferable default as a missing user decision. (2) Halting all work when only one branch is blocked. (3) Escalating for formatting decisions covered by style packs. (4) Escalating without a structured blocker_report.json. (5) Using escalation to avoid making reasonable editorial judgment calls. (6) Escalating the same blocker twice after a default has been applied.
